```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6)
set.seed(42)
```

# Input and scope

Each column of the Part 2 effect matrix is one perturbation-level log2 CPM difference from the non-targeting aggregate. The columns summarize selected, sufficiently represented perturbations from one public experiment. Cell-level DE, raw-count aggregate profiles, and effect vectors have distinct statistical units.

```{r packages}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(pheatmap)
library(ggrepel)
library(tibble)
```

```{r input}
delta <- readRDS("data/processed/03_perturbation_effect_matrix.rds")
pseudobulk <- readRDS("data/processed/03_pseudobulk_raw_counts.rds")
stopifnot(is.matrix(delta), all(colnames(delta) %in% colnames(pseudobulk)))
X <- t(delta)
cat("Perturbations x genes:", paste(dim(X), collapse=" x "), "\n")
```

### Interpretation

Each of the 12 rows represents a perturbation-level effect vector across the same 2,000 genes. These vectors summarize aggregate differences from control and are distinct from individual-cell measurements or replicate-aware estimates.

# Cosine similarity

Cosine similarity measures agreement in response direction and is less sensitive than Euclidean distance to overall response magnitude. Zero-magnitude vectors are rejected because their cosine is undefined.

```{r cosine}
norms <- sqrt(rowSums(X^2))
stopifnot(all(norms > 0))
unit <- sweep(X, 1, norms, "/")
cos_sim <- tcrossprod(unit)
diag(cos_sim) <- 1
pairs <- as.data.frame(as.table(cos_sim)) |>
  setNames(c("target_a", "target_b", "cosine")) |>
  filter(as.character(target_a) < as.character(target_b)) |>
  arrange(desc(cosine))
print(head(pairs, 10))
pheatmap(cos_sim, border_color=NA, main="Cosine similarity of K562 perturbation effects")
write.csv(pairs, "results/04_response_similarity_pairs.csv", row.names=FALSE)
```

### Key finding

DONSON–RRM2 has the highest cosine similarity (0.696) among the analyzed target pairs, indicating the most similar response direction across the selected genes. Cosine similarity emphasizes direction rather than absolute magnitude. It does not establish a shared pathway, direct interaction, or mechanism.

# Perturbation-level PCA

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(X, center=TRUE, scale.=FALSE)
pca_df <- data.frame(perturbation=rownames(pca$x), PC1=pca$x[,1], PC2=pca$x[,2])
variance <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
cat("PC1 variance (%):", round(variance[1], 2), "PC2 variance (%):", round(variance[2], 2), "\n")
print(pca_df)
ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, label=perturbation)) + geom_point(size=2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(max.overlaps=Inf) +
  labs(x=paste0("PC1 (", round(variance[1],1), "%)"), y=paste0("PC2 (", round(variance[2],1), "%)")) + theme_minimal()
write.csv(pca_df, "results/04_perturbation_PCA.csv", row.names=FALSE)
```

### Interpretation

Perturbation-level PC1 and PC2 account for 23.22% and 19.73% of variation among these effect vectors. Their plot summarizes differences across the focused 12-target cohort; point distances can reflect both response direction and magnitude and need not imply mechanistic relatedness.

# Response clustering

```{r cluster}
distance <- 1-cos_sim
distance[distance < 0] <- 0
hc <- hclust(as.dist(distance), method="average")
plot(hc, main="Hierarchical clustering of perturbation effects", xlab="", sub="")
cluster_id <- cutree(hc, k=3)
cluster_table <- data.frame(perturbation=names(cluster_id), response_cluster=unname(cluster_id))
print(cluster_table |> arrange(response_cluster, perturbation))
write.csv(cluster_table, "results/04_response_clusters.csv", row.names=FALSE)
```

### Interpretation

Average-linkage clustering groups similar response directions into clusters of six, five, and one perturbation. This grouping can guide follow-up comparisons, but the three-cluster cut was chosen for inspection. The singleton CHMP6 represents an outlying response pattern in this cohort, not a new biological subtype.

# Genes associated with response clusters

```{r programs}
programs <- bind_rows(lapply(sort(unique(cluster_id)), function(k) {
  members <- names(cluster_id)[cluster_id == k]
  others <- setdiff(colnames(delta), members)
  mean_member <- rowMeans(delta[, members, drop=FALSE])
  mean_other <- rowMeans(delta[, others, drop=FALSE])
  difference <- mean_member - mean_other
  data.frame(response_cluster=k, gene=names(difference), mean_effect=mean_member,
             contrast_to_other_clusters=difference, n_perturbations=length(members)) |>
    slice_max(abs(contrast_to_other_clusters), n=15, with_ties=FALSE)
}))
print(programs)
write.csv(programs, "results/04_response_cluster_programs.csv", row.names=FALSE)
pheatmap(delta[unique(programs$gene), , drop=FALSE], scale="none", border_color=NA,
         main="Genes distinguishing descriptive response clusters")
```

### Interpretation

Ranked genes distinguish each cluster's mean effect from the other selected perturbations and suggest descriptive response programs. Cluster 3 contains only CHMP6, so its ranked genes describe one target rather than a shared program. All contrasts use a shared control and lack biological replicates.

# Save

```{r save}
saveRDS(list(X=X, cosine=cos_sim, pca=pca, clusters=cluster_table, programs=programs),
        "data/processed/04_perturbation_embeddings.rds")
```

## Key results

```{r key-results}
cat("Perturbations:", nrow(X), "effect genes:", ncol(X), "response clusters:", length(unique(cluster_id)), "\n")
cat("Highest cosine pair:", as.character(pairs$target_a[1]), "/", as.character(pairs$target_b[1]), round(pairs$cosine[1], 3), "\n")
cat("PCA variance (%):", round(variance[1], 2), "and", round(variance[2], 2), "\n")
```

- **Effect representation:** 12 perturbation vectors across 2,000 genes support target-level comparisons.
- **Response similarity:** DONSON–RRM2 has the highest cosine similarity (0.696), indicating aligned response direction.
- **PCA:** PC1 and PC2 explain 23.22% and 19.73% of vector variation in this cohort.
- **Clustering:** response groups contain six, five, and one target; the CHMP6 singleton is an outlier, not a shared program.
